extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, scientific method, and evidence evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating testimonial and observational evidence in inductive reasoning — when to believe extraordinary claims (miracles, coincidences, novel kinds) and how to separate direct observation from inference. Covers principles for weighing prior improbability, alternative hypotheses, and witnesses’ reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles require antecedent probability of the supernatural cause
rubrics_metrics.description: A miracle is not a contradiction to the law of cause and effect but a new effect supposed to be produced by the introduction of a new cause; the only antecedent improbability ascribable to the miracle is the improbability that any such cause existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus to accept a miracle one must have antecedent probability that a being or cause with the requisite supernatural power existed; otherwise the alternative hypothesis of some unknown natural cause remains viable.

rubrics_metrics.name: No evidence can prove a miracle to someone without prior belief in supernatural agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: No evidence can prove a miracle to any one who did not previously believe the existence of a being or beings with supernatural power, or who believes himself to have full proof that the character of the Being recognized is inconsistent with intervening on the occasion in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People who already believe in such beings weigh supernatural vs unknown natural hypotheses and judge which is more probable given the circumstances; non-believers will not be convinced by the same evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary claims that conflict with general uniformity need extraordinary antecedent probability
rubrics_metrics.description: With knowledge of the general uniformity of nature, there is a general presumption against divine (or special) interpositions not operating through general laws — an antecedent improbability exists for every miracle which requires extraordinary strength of antecedent probability from special circumstances to outweigh it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a reported fact conflicts with well-established uniformities, accept it only if the special circumstances provide sufficiently strong antecedent probability (e.g., multiple independent, highly credible confirmations).

rubrics_metrics.name: When an alleged fact conflicts with a firmly ascertained causal law, judge by probability of an adequate counteracting cause
rubrics_metrics.description: The assertion that a cause has been defeated of an effect connected with it by a completely ascertained law of causation is to be disbelieved or not according to the probability that there existed an adequate counteracting cause in that instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate this by considering known causes capable of counteracting the given cause and the prior knowledge of their frequency or rarity; focus on probability of their having existed at the particular time and place.

rubrics_metrics.name: For unknown counteracting causes judge only their presence at the time/place, not their general existence
rubrics_metrics.description: We are not required to pronounce on the probability of unknown causes existing in nature generally, but only on the probability of their having existed at the time and place alleged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether such a cause could have existed without leaving other marks, and whether its prior non-manifestation elsewhere makes its presence in this instance improbable; use available circumstantial information to assess this localized probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegations of a new Kind (violating co-existence uniformities) should be provisionally accepted if plausible and awaiting confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions that purport to establish a new Kind are not inherently incredible unless the improbability that such a variety would have remained undiscovered is greater than that of error or mendacity in the witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credible persons reporting unexplored places require confirmation from subsequent observers unless alleged properties violate known properties of larger Kinds (i.e., disjoining properties always found together), in which case greater skepticism or provisional disbelief is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to most general laws (number, extension, causation) are absolutely incredible
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformities true of all things whatever — e.g., laws of number, extension, and the law of causation itself — are admissible as universal truths with credence proportioned to their generality; exceptions to these are absolutely and permanently incredible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims contradicting these very general laws should be treated as impossible (total impossibility) rather than merely improbable; such claims demand proof sufficient to shake belief in the law itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violations of more specific laws are contextually impossible unless special causes existed
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations of special or less general laws are properly described as 'impossible in the circumstances of the case' unless some counteracting cause existed which did not exist in the particular case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply contextual judgment: determine whether circumstances required for violation could have occurred; if not, treat the claim as effectively impossible without extraordinary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspend judgment for anomalous claims that neither contradict major laws nor are decisively corroborated
rubrics_metrics.description: If testimony in favor of an anomaly presents no suspicious circumstances and does not contradict universal laws or very comprehensive generalizations, a cautious person should neither admit nor reject it but wait for confirmation from other unconnected sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use suspension of judgment as a default pending further independent confirmation; avoid premature acceptance or rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize testimony for signs of fallacious appearances, epidemic delusion, or vested interests
rubrics_metrics.description: In many records where many credible witnesses testified to something that turned out untrue, there were circumstances rendering testimony untrustworthy: fallacious appearances, epidemic delusion (contagion of popular feeling), or strong interests such as religious zeal, party feeling, vanity, or passion for the marvelous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating testimony, actively search for such motives or psychological/social mechanisms that could explain widespread but false testimony; their presence lowers credence significantly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish improbability before the fact from improbability after it
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an important distinction between the improbability of a mere guess being right (improbability before the fact) and the improbability of an alleged fact being true once reported (improbability after it). Many events unlikely beforehand are not incredible once reported if they are not contrary to induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing testimony, avoid rejecting a reported event solely because it was unlikely beforehand; instead consider whether the reported fact contradicts known regularities or whether its occurrence was plausible in the situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unusualness alone is insufficient ground for disbelief when the situation makes unusual events inevitable
rubrics_metrics.description: The unusualness (immense preponderance of chances against) of an event is no reason to disbelieve it if the nature of the case renders it certain that something unusual must have occurred (e.g., a die must show some face).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the reported unusual outcome is one of many mutually exclusive possibilities and whether observation of some specific outcome was inevitable; that removes the force of prior improbability as a reason to disbelieve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coincidences may require stronger evidence, but assessment must be case-specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Coincidences — peculiar and unexpected regularities — are often regarded as more improbable and thus requiring stronger evidence; however whether they do so depends on first principles and the particular structure of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine motives for falsehood (coincidences excite wonder and motives to fabricate), the distribution of possible errors, and whether witnesses are of the type who would be especially careful about extraordinary occurrences. Do not apply a blanket rule; assess the comparative probability of testimony being delivered if the fact were untrue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute observed regularity to causes with greater efficacy when comparing causal hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: When a highly regular result occurs (e.g., repeated sixes), it is more likely to be produced by a cause which in the circumstances would very likely produce that result (design, unfairness) than by chance; we should prefer the cause most likely to produce the observed effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate comparative likelihoods of competing causes given the observed regularity. Use principles like Laplace’s (superior efficacy can outweigh antecedent improbability after a few observations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility of testimony depends on structure of alternatives and likely error modes (Laplace critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: The credibility of a witness’s assertion is affected by how many alternatives the witness could have mistaken or chosen among and how errors are likely to be distributed; e.g., an assertion that a specific number was drawn among 1000 possibilities differs from a binary black/white report because false announcements distribute differently among alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying probabilistic arguments, ensure the modelling assumptions match the real situation: whether the witness knows the distribution, whether alternatives are distinguishable, and whether errors/biases connect to particular outcomes. Avoid simplistic application of examples that assume uniform error behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: The witness’s task complexity affects error rates: fewer possible errors can reduce mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: A person is far less likely to err when only one form of error is possible than when many errors are possible; in many 'binary' observations a witness may make fewer mistakes than in multi-option reporting situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the cognitive/perceptual demands on the observer and whether the reporting task simplifies or multiplies potential errors. This affects how much testimony supports a rare-event claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate direct sensation (observation) from inferential judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The sole condition for relying on observation is that what is supposed to have been observed shall really have been observed; observation properly extends only to sensations, while most propositions about objects are inferences from those sensations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating reported observations, ask whether the reporter is describing direct sensory impressions or has already made inferential attributions (e.g., 'I heard a sound' vs 'I heard a man's voice'); treat inferential elements with additional skepticism and require justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat so-called errors of sense as errors of inference, not faulty sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent 'errors of sense' (optical illusions, hallucinations, misidentification) are usually not failures of the sensory organs but erroneous inferences from genuine sensations — the sensations are real, the judgment about their cause may be mistaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate alternative causal explanations for the sensations (optical effects, hallucination, resemblance, dream states) before rejecting the sensory report; training and reflection can help separate perception from habitual inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation reports are often compound (sensations + inference); require scrutiny of the inferential portion
rubrics_metrics.description: What we commonly call observation is usually a compound result where a small part is direct perception and the larger part is inference (e.g., recognizing a voice, identifying a person).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand clarity from observers about what they literally perceived versus what they inferred. Encourage trained methods of observation and reflectiveness to reduce conflation of perception and inference.
